lead: A list can grow at its right end and shrink from either end. That makes one list serve two classic containers. Add with append and remove with pop() and you get a stack: last in, first out. Add with append and remove with pop(0) and you get a queue: first in, first out. Undo buttons, browser back navigation, bracket checkers, printer jobs and ticket lines all use one of these two patterns.
prereq: You need 3.3 for append, pop and list indexing.

sections.h3: A stack removes the newest item

blocks.text: A stack is a container with one working end, called the top. Push puts an item on top. Pop removes and returns the top item. Peek reads the top without removing it. The rule is last in, first out (LIFO): the item pushed most recently is the first one popped.

A Python list already has every operation a stack needs. Push x with s.append(x). Pop with top = s.pop(). Peek with top = s[-1]. Test empty with len(s) == 0. No class is required here; Unit 4 shows the class version.

items: Push x: s.append(x) adds x at the right end.
Pop: top = s.pop() removes and returns the rightmost item.
Peek: top = s[-1] reads the rightmost item without removing it.
Empty test: len(s) == 0 is True when the stack holds no items.

blocks.text: Undo in an editor is a stack: each edit is pushed, and undo pops the latest edit. The browser back button works the same way. A bracket checker pushes every opening bracket and pops on every closing bracket. A function call stack, which Unit 2 covers under recursion, also follows LIFO.

sections.h3: A queue removes the oldest item

blocks.text: A queue is a container with two ends: rear for entry and front for exit. Enqueue adds at the rear. Dequeue removes and returns from the front. The rule is first in, first out (FIFO): the item that waited longest leaves first.
On a list, enqueue x with q.append(x). Dequeue with first = q.pop(0). The call pop(0) removes index 0 and shifts every remaining item one place left, so it costs O(n) time on a list of n items.

blocks.where: n is the number of items in q; every item after index 0 shifts one place left, so the work grows in proportion to n.

blocks.text: When a queue is long and dequeues are frequent, that shifting matters. collections.deque provides append and popleft, both O(1). Only a few syllabi require deque at this stage.
A printer queue is FIFO: the first document sent is printed first. A ticket counter line is FIFO. Breadth-first search, covered in Unit 6, uses a queue to visit nodes level by level.

sections.h3: Empty pops and the right end

blocks.text: Both pop() and pop(0) raise IndexError when the list is empty. Check len(s) == 0 or not s before popping. The same check protects a queue.

The two patterns differ only in which end they remove from. Stack: append right, pop right. Queue: append right, pop left. Mixing them gives the wrong order. Using s.pop(0) as a stack is not LIFO. Using q.pop() as a queue is not FIFO.

Bracket matching: scan a string. Push each opening bracket. On a closing bracket, pop and compare. If the popped bracket is not the matching opener, or the stack is empty, the string is invalid. At the end the stack must be empty.

figure.caption: Push adds at the right end and pop takes from the same end, so the last item pushed is the first one out.

spec.title: a list used as a stack
spec.aria: A stack row 10, 20, 30 with a pointer on the top item, and after one pop a row 10, 20 with the pointer moved one cell left.

examples.question: A list s = [] is used as a stack. Run s.append(10), s.append(20), s.append(30), then p = s.pop(), then read s[-1]. Next a list q = [] is used as a queue. Run q.append('A'), q.append('B'), q.append('C'), then r = q.pop(0). Give p, s, s[-1], r and q.
steps: Start s = []. After append(10): s = [10]. After append(20): s = [10, 20]. After append(30): s = [10, 20, 30]. Top is index 2.
p = s.pop() removes the last item, 30. So p = 30 and s = [10, 20]. The new top is index 1.
s[-1] reads the last item without removal, so s[-1] = 20.
Start q = []. After the appends: q = ['A', 'B', 'C']. Front is index 0.
r = q.pop(0) removes index 0, 'A'. So r = 'A' and q = ['B', 'C']. Length of q is 2.
examples.check:
s = []
s.append(10); s.append(20); s.append(30)
p = s.pop()
print(p)
print(s[-1])
q = []
q.append('A'); q.append('B'); q.append('C')
r = q.pop(0)
print(len(q))

traps: pop() removes the newest item for a stack; pop(0) removes the oldest item for a queue. Swapping them reverses the order.
pop(0) costs O(n) on a list because every remaining item shifts left; pop() at the end costs O(1).
Both pop() and pop(0) raise IndexError on an empty list; check len(s) == 0 or not s first.
append adds at the right end for both patterns. A queue is not made by insert(0, x), which also costs O(n).
A stack is LIFO and a queue is FIFO; exam questions often ask which end is removed, not which end is added.

quiz.q: Which list method pushes an item onto a stack, and which method pops it?
Which list call removes the front item of a queue?
Why does q.pop(0) cost O(n) while q.pop() costs O(1)?
quiz.a: pop(0) removes index 0 and shifts every remaining item one place left, so n-1 moves; pop() removes the last item with no shift.

quiz.q: Start s = [4, 5]. Run s.append(6), s.pop(), s.append(7). Give s and the value returned by s[-1].
quiz.a: After append(6): s = [4, 5, 6]. pop returns 6, s = [4, 5]. append(7): s = [4, 5, 7]. s[-1] is 7.

quiz.q: Start q = []. Append 1, 2, 3. Then q.pop(0) twice. Give the returned values and q.
quiz.a: First pop(0) returns 1, q = [2, 3]. Second returns 2, q = [3].

quiz.q: A program uses q.pop(0) in a loop on a list of 10,000 items. Why might collections.deque be faster, and which two deque methods replace append and pop(0)?
quiz.a: pop(0) shifts all remaining items each time, O(n) per dequeue; deque.popleft() is O(1) at the left and append is O(1) at the right. Replace q.append with dq.append and q.pop(0) with dq.popleft().

quiz.q: A bracket checker pushes every opening bracket and pops on a closing bracket. What does an empty stack at a closing bracket mean, and what must be true at the end?
quiz.a: Empty stack means no unmatched opener exists for that closer, so the string is invalid. At the end the stack must be empty; otherwise some opener was never closed.

quiz.q: State the LIFO and FIFO rules in one sentence each.
quiz.a: LIFO: the item added most recently is removed first. FIFO: the item added earliest is removed first.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real programs often need a queue that many threads can use safely; Python's queue.Queue adds locking around FIFO operations. Double-ended queues also support undo/redo history and sliding-window algorithms. Search for "collections.deque", "breadth-first search" and "producer consumer queue" to go further.
